title: The State of Public Education in 2026 in Five Charts
author: Julia H. Kaufman
text:
The State of Public Education in 2026 in Five Charts

Commentary
Aug 17, 2026

Photo by Goodboy Picture Company/Getty Images

By Julia H. Kaufman, Melissa Kay Diliberti, Elizabeth D. Steiner, Benjamin K. Master, Ashley Woo

RAND has spent more than a decade surveying educators across the United States and has now expanded this effort to include the perspectives of students and parents. Our seven standing panels of teachers, principals, superintendents, students, parents, adults from the general population, and veterans offer one-of-a-kind insight into the state of American public education.

Among the hundreds of survey questions we fielded this past year, the results depicted in these five charts stood out the most.

They have a common thread: American educators and students are navigating real headwinds. Monitoring our survey data is an important step toward addressing these challenges.

Teachers Are Still Burning Out, and Managing Student Behavior Is a Top Source of Their Stress

Every year since 2021, RAND's State of the American Teacher project has asked a nationally representative sample of public-school teachers how they are doing. Every year, teachers have reported worse well-being than similar working adults. This past year is no exception: In 2026, U.S. teachers reported poorer well-being on every indicator we track.

The top source of job-related stress is managing student behavior, followed by low pay and working too many hours. Those pressures are not hard to explain: Teachers feel the effects of chronic absenteeism and poor student mental health every day. The toll shows up in how teachers think about their futures. In 2026, only one in four said they planned to stay in the profession as long as they were able. Persistently poor teacher well-being matters not only for educators themselves but also for the students who depend on having a stable, experienced teacher.

Two-Thirds of Students Agree That Using AI More for Schoolwork Harms Their Critical Thinking

Despite misgivings about AI harming critical thinking, students are using AI tools for homework at growing rates. Repeated nationally representative surveys of youth show that the share of students who are using AI for help with their homework has increased over the last 18 months. That alone might be unsurprising; AI tools are everywhere.

What's more striking is what students said about the use of such tools: Sixty-seven percent of youth surveyed in December 2025 agreed or strongly agreed that the more students use AI for their schoolwork, the more it will harm their critical thinking skills.

Skepticism about AI is high across grade levels, although older students were most likely to strongly agree about potential negative effects on critical thinking. The sharpest skeptics, however, are students who are not currently using AI for help with their homework.

Chronic Absenteeism Is Falling—but Remains Well Above Pre-Pandemic Levels

One of the pandemic's most consequential legacies for American schools is chronic absenteeism—missing 10 percent or more of school days in a year. Rates of absenteeism spiked following the pandemic, with rates initially twice the pre-pandemic norm.

Our latest data reflect some good news: Chronic absenteeism declined over the past year. But there's bad news, too: In the five years since schools reopened, absenteeism remains well above where it stood before the pandemic, with the highest rates in urban school districts.

It's not clear that attendance norms will fully reset on their own. That uncertainty matters, because chronic absenteeism rates aren't just a number. Higher rates predict lower academic achievement and higher dropout risk, meaning every school year in which rates remain elevated represents a real cost to students' futures.

The decline in absenteeism is reason for cautious optimism, but this issue still demands continued attention from school and district leaders.

Students and Smartphones: More-Restrictive Policies Seem to Mitigate—Not Eliminate—the Problem

Policies restricting students' cell phone use during the school day have spread rapidly across U.S. public schools, driven by increasing concerns about students' overreliance on their smartphones and evidence linking smartphone use to poor mental health and distracted learning.

But not all phone policies are the same. Local policies vary considerably in how strict they are and when and where phone use is actually prohibited. We identified five distinct types of school cell phone policies across U.S. public schools and examined how each relates to how often students check their phones.

We found that policies that are more restrictive about where and when students can use their phones are associated with reduced percentages of students checking their devices. This result offers a clear signal to school and district leaders that the effectiveness of cell phone policies likely depends on the degree of restrictiveness.

Pre-K Teachers Lack Adequate Materials to Support Children's Diverse Learning Needs

The materials a pre-K teacher uses shape what children learn and how. Yet a nationally representative survey found that pre-K teachers in public schools are often mixing and matching different instructional materials, likely because no single material adequately addresses the wide variety of needs in their classrooms. Eighty-five percent of pre-K teachers reported using multiple instructional materials, often combining comprehensive curriculum materials with many other resources.

That mixing and matching reflects a gap: Only about half of pre-K teachers said their materials were adequate for supporting children with diverse learning needs, such as children with disabilities or English learners. That gap is illustrated by the higher proportions of teachers trying to serve those diverse needs by using materials of unknown quality, such as materials they create themselves and those available through the website Teachers Pay Teachers.

The earliest years of education, when foundational skills in language, literacy, and numeracy take root, is precisely the wrong time to leave teachers without the tools they need to support every child.

As schools open their doors this fall, it's clear that students, teachers, and principals are navigating many challenges. Tracking those challenges with rigorous data—fielded consistently and shared publicly—is how we at RAND give educators, policymakers, and families the information they need to meet this moment.

Tracking American public education like this requires consistent, long-term investment in asking the right questions. RAND builds and maintains the infrastructure to do that: nationally representative panels that produce timely, comparable data year after year. No single set of surveys can capture everything, but our work can provide some answers to the questions that matter most. We intend to keep asking.
